children: Tax-loss harvesting — selling a security that fell in price in order to use the loss to offset gains elsewhere in a portfolio — was a significant opportunity for bond investors in the third quarter.
That is thanks to a rapid rise in yields, as bond prices move inversely to interest rates. Many investors took advantage of that opportunity, particularly in municipal bonds.

In fact, so many investors sold their munis that it may have exacerbated already painful losses. Munis fell 6.4% in the third quarter compared with about a 3% decline for corporate bonds and Treasuries. Bond prices have since rebounded, so tax-loss opportunities are now less available. Still, the deluge of tax-related selling sheds light on how two important investing trends — the popularity of tax-advantaged automatic investing programs and the growth of exchange-traded funds — are reshaping market dynamics.

Tax-loss harvesting activity in municipal bonds is a familiar headwind whenever municipal bonds have a rough year, "but this year was unprecedented," says Jeff Timlin, lead portfolio manager for municipal bond strategies at Sage Advisory. "I've never seen anything like it." Trading volume in munis in September nearly doubled from the average of the first seven months of 2026, says Brian Barney, a portfolio manager on the fixed-income team at Parametric.

"It was kind of off the charts," says Duane McAllister, a senior portfolio manager and co-leader of the municipal sector at Baird. "We've had more trading related to tax-loss harvesting than we've ever seen, and the interesting thing is that tax losses weren't nearly as large as they have been at other points in time," he says, referencing selloffs during the pandemic in 2020 and in April 2025, after President Donald Trump announced tariffs on so-called Liberation Day.

For starters, there are a lot of investors looking to diversify out of highly appreciated stocks who could use those losses to offset the gains. Plus, the growth in automated tax-loss harvesting offered by many asset managers is a likely factor. Parametric's offering, available to accounts over $125,000, automatically looks for tax-loss harvesting opportunities when a bond has declined more than 3%, says Barney.

Another trend at work: Investors are moving from mutual funds to more tax-efficient exchange-traded funds. Tax-loss harvesting may have created the impetus for some investors to make the switch, since exchanging an active mutual fund for an index ETF generally avoids the wash-sale rule. (You can't take a tax deduction for a loss on the sale of a security if you purchased another security that is essentially the same 30 days before or after the sale.)
Since the beginning of September, open-end mutual funds experienced net outflows of nearly $30 billion, while muni ETFs picked up $20 billion in inflows, Barney says.

Tax-loss harvesting happened in other areas of the bond market, but it didn't have the same impact as on the muni market, says Barney. That's because the corporate bond market is larger and more liquid. Also, taxable bonds are often held in tax-deferred accounts, where tax-loss selling doesn't make sense.

While the tax-loss harvesting opportunity is largely over, the impact of all that activity remains, says Sage's Timlin. Munis' after-tax yields "were as attractive as they had been in 20-plus years," he says, but investors looking to buy individual bonds when trading activity was at a peak found it challenging.

While there are minimal transaction costs for trading in ETFs these days, fund managers argue there are other hidden costs for muni investors. For example, the data suggest that investors bought index funds as a placeholder, planning to get back into an actively managed fund when the wash-sale rule was no longer a factor. Now they are effectively stuck in them since selling would trigger a short-term gain, which could erase the benefit of harvesting the tax loss, says Timlin.

Plus, they may not be in an optimal position in terms of security selection or the overall interest-rate sensitivity of their muni portfolio. The iShares National Muni Bond ETF is underperforming about 60% of municipal bond funds year to date, according to Morningstar.
McAllister calls that "leakage." He says: "If you stay in the new investment, it may not be exactly what you wanted. There is a cost, but it is hard to quantify."
